topic: Measuring the incumbent process before setting an eval bar
stem: A national parks agency is starting work on a Claude step that drafts replies to public consultation submissions. Today two policy officers write every reply by hand. The delivery team wants to begin prompt engineering this week and has asked the eval lead to nominate an acceptance threshold. What should the eval lead do before nominating a number?

options.text: Measure the existing manual process on the same items — officer throughput, and how often two officers independently rate the same draft acceptable.
Set the bar at 95% acceptable, which is the standard the agency already applies to the published correspondence it sends under its own name.
Build the first stable prompt version, see where it lands on the eval, and adopt that score as the baseline for every later version to improve on.
Decline to set a numeric bar and rely on officer sign-off of every draft during the pilot, deferring the eval until volumes make automation worthwhile.

explanation.correct: An acceptance threshold is only meaningful against a comparator, and here one already exists in the officers. Two facts change everything about what number is reasonable: what the officers' own throughput is, and how often two of them agree that a given draft is acceptable. If independent officers agree only four times in five, a 95% target is not achievable by anything, human or model, because the construct itself is not that reproducible. Measuring the incumbent also gives the agency the before-and-after it will need when someone asks whether the investment paid off.

distractors.B: Importing a standard from published correspondence sets a bar without knowing whether the current process clears it. It is also a different construct: a draft reviewed by an officer before publication is not held to the same standard as the published text.
distractors.C: This makes the first implementation the definition of adequate. The threshold then encodes whatever the initial prompt happened to achieve, and nobody can say whether that is good enough for the consultation process or merely where the work stopped.
distractors.D: Full sign-off is a reasonable pilot control and should probably run regardless. On its own it produces no comparable measurement, so when the agency later wants to reduce the review burden there is no evidence to support doing so.

explanation.concept: Baseline first, then set the bar. Measure the process being replaced on the same items and, where the task is subjective, measure how much two competent humans agree. Human agreement is the practical ceiling on any automated score for that construct, and a target above it is a target nobody can hit or verify.
explanation.tip: When a stem contains an existing manual process, the missing measurement is almost always the incumbent's performance. Targets set without a baseline are the most common source of unshippable acceptance criteria.

topic: Giving an LLM judge a reference answer to grade against
stem: A subtitling company grades Spanish subtitle translations with an LLM judge that sees the English source and the candidate translation and returns a 1–5 quality rating. Reviewers report that the judge rates almost everything 4 or 5, including segments where a domain specialist can point at a clear meaning error. The company has a library of professionally produced reference translations for a subset of its catalogue. What change to the grading design would most improve discrimination?

options.text: Widen the rating scale from 1–5 to 1–10, giving the judge more room to separate the many segments it currently rates 4 or 5 alike.
Supply the professional reference alongside the source and candidate, and require the judge to name meaning divergences before it rates.
Replace the judge with an n-gram overlap score against the professional reference translation, which is objective, cheap and fully reproducible.
Keep the reference-free setup but decompose the 1–5 rating into three sub-dimensions — accuracy, fluency and timing — and sum them.

explanation.correct: Without a reference the judge has to reconstruct what a good translation of this segment would be, and where it lacks the domain knowledge to do that it defaults to fluency, which almost everything passes. The professional translation supplies the missing anchor, and forcing the judge to name divergences before rating converts a holistic impression into an evidence-backed verdict a reviewer can check. The library covers only a subset of the catalogue, which is fine: reference-based grading on that subset can be used to validate the reference-free judge everywhere else.

distractors.A: A wider scale does not create discrimination the judge cannot perceive. It will use a narrow band of the larger range, comparability with every previous run is lost, and the underlying problem — no anchor for what good looks like on this segment — is untouched.
distractors.C: Overlap scoring against a single reference punishes legitimate alternative phrasings and is insensitive to meaning errors that happen to reuse the reference's words. It is defensible as a cheap screening layer beneath a judge, not as the grade.
distractors.D: Decomposition improves interpretability and attributability, and is worth doing anyway. It does not give the judge the information it is missing, so three sub-dimensions rated without an anchor will be three generous ratings instead of one.

explanation.concept: Reference-based grading is markedly more discriminating than reference-free grading on tasks requiring knowledge the judge may lack. Where references exist for part of the corpus, use them both to grade that part and to validate a reference-free judge on the rest. Requiring the judge to cite specific evidence before scoring is what makes its verdict auditable.
explanation.tip: A judge that rates nearly everything at the top of its scale is usually short of information, not short of scale. Ask what the judge would need in order to know the answer is wrong.

topic: Choosing a grading format that resolves a small quality gap
stem: A pharmaceutical company's medical-information team must choose between two prompt versions for drafting responses to healthcare-professional enquiries. Both are graded with a four-level absolute rubric, and across 500 items both land on the same level for 96% of items, giving effectively identical scores. The team's own reviewers, reading a handful side by side, consistently prefer one version. The decision has to be defended to a governance committee. What should the eval lead do?

options.text: Grade each output five times with the same four-level rubric and average, so the discrete levels become a finer-grained continuous score.
Widen the absolute rubric from four levels to ten, giving the small differences between the two versions somewhere to land.
Present the two outputs for each item side by side with the order randomised, and report the win, tie and loss distribution across the 500 items.
Conclude the versions are equivalent on quality and decide on cost, since a rubric that cannot separate them is evidence there is nothing to separate.

explanation.correct: The reviewers' side-by-side preference is the clue: the difference is real but smaller than one rubric level, so an absolute scale cannot see it. Pairwise comparison asks the easier question — which of these two is better — which graders answer far more sensitively than they answer where does this one sit on a scale. Randomising order keeps position out of the result, and reporting ties explicitly gives the governance committee the honest picture: a win rate plus the share of items on which the two are indistinguishable.

distractors.A: Averaging repeated grades reduces noise around each item's level and is worth doing generally. If both outputs genuinely occupy the same level on nearly every item, averaging returns the same number more precisely. Resolution is the limit here, not noise.
distractors.B: Ten levels without a written anchor for each is not finer measurement, it is arbitrary placement. Graders use unanchored wide scales inconsistently, which adds variance and can make the comparison less sensitive rather than more.
distractors.D: This is the tempting reading and it is backwards. An instrument that buckets both variants into the same level has not demonstrated equivalence, it has demonstrated it cannot resolve the question. Concluding equivalence from a coarse instrument is how a real improvement gets discarded.

explanation.concept: Match the grading format to the size of the difference you need to detect. Absolute rubrics are right for tracking a level against a standard; pairwise comparison is right for choosing between close candidates. When an absolute rubric returns a tie and humans do not, the rubric is the limiting factor.
explanation.tip: The detail that reviewers reliably prefer one version while the rubric cannot separate them is doing all the work. It rules out equivalence and points squarely at instrument resolution.

topic: Cohort-level reporting to surface a small-segment regression
stem: A European rail operator runs a Claude-based passenger enquiry assistant in four languages. English is 71% of traffic, German 18%, French 7% and Dutch 4%. The overall eval pass rate has held steady at 89% across the last two releases, but complaints from Dutch-speaking passengers have roughly tripled since the most recent one. The eval lead is asked why the suite did not catch it. What is the correct change to the eval design?

options.text: Keep the aggregate as the headline and handle the complaints as a support issue, since they are not yet corroborated by any eval measurement.
Increase the overall eval set size until the aggregate pass rate is sensitive enough to register a regression in a single language.
Add a language-quality criterion to the judging rubric, so the aggregate pass rate falls whenever the output in any of the four languages degrades.
Report the pass rate per language cohort with its own interval, sizing each cohort to detect a meaningful move rather than to match traffic share.

explanation.correct: A traffic-weighted aggregate is designed not to move when a 4% segment degrades: even a catastrophic collapse in Dutch shifts the overall figure by a few points at most, and a moderate one is invisible. The suite has to carry a cohort that is large enough to measure in its own right, which means deliberately over-sampling Dutch relative to its traffic share and reporting it separately. That is a decision about what the eval is for — detecting harm to any segment — rather than about estimating a single population average.

distractors.A: The complaints are the corroboration, and they arrived because the eval was blind. Deferring to a support process leaves the suite unable to catch the same failure on the next release, which is the specific thing the eval lead was asked about.
distractors.B: A larger sample estimates the same weighted average more precisely. Precision is not the problem: the aggregate would still be 71% English by construction, and a Dutch regression would still move it by a fraction of a point.
distractors.C: A new criterion changes what is graded but still rolls up into one number across all four languages. A criterion averaged across cohorts conceals cohort differences in exactly the way the pass rate already does.

explanation.concept: An aggregate metric is a weighted average and it will always be dominated by the largest segment. If the system must not fail any segment, each segment needs its own measurement, sized for its own detectable effect rather than for its traffic share. Decide the reporting cohorts before the incident, from who could be harmed.
explanation.tip: When a stem lists segment proportions, compute what a collapse in the smallest one would do to the headline. If the answer is less than the noise, the item is about cohort reporting.

topic: Defining property of a golden dataset
stem: What property most distinguishes a golden dataset from any other collection of eval items?

options.text: It is larger than the working eval set, which is what allows the narrower confidence intervals quoted on the reported score.
It is constructed to cover the edge cases and adversarial inputs a system has not yet encountered in production traffic.
Its labels are established independently of the system under test and treated as authoritative, so any disagreement is a system error.
It is refreshed at every release so that it always reflects the current production traffic distribution and item mix.

explanation.correct: The word golden refers to the labels, not the items. What makes the set usable as a reference is that its answers were determined without reference to what the system produces — by domain experts, by adjudicated annotation, or by ground truth recorded elsewhere — and are accepted as correct for the purpose of scoring. That authority is exactly what permits the asymmetric reading of a disagreement: the system is wrong, not the label. Sets whose labels came from the system, or from a single unreviewed annotator, cannot support that reading.

distractors.A: Size is unrelated and often runs the other way. Authoritative labelling is expensive, so golden sets are frequently small and are supplemented by larger, more cheaply labelled sets for routine runs.
distractors.B: Deliberate edge-case coverage describes a stress or adversarial set. A golden set may include edge cases, but its defining feature is label provenance rather than how the items were chosen.
distractors.D: Constant refresh describes a set whose job is to track the current distribution. A golden set is deliberately stable, because its value lies in being the same fixed reference across many system versions.

explanation.concept: Judge a reference dataset by the provenance of its labels: who decided them, on what evidence, with what adjudication, and independently of what. Everything else — size, difficulty, coverage, freshness — is a property of a particular eval set and can be traded. Label authority cannot.
explanation.tip: Definitional recall items usually offer three properties that are merely common and one that is constitutive. Ask which property, if removed, would stop the thing being what it is called.

topic: Re-baselining a trend when the judge model changes
stem: A professional-services firm has reported a monthly quality trend for its engagement-summary feature for two years, graded by a judge pinned to one model version. The firm's own model-lifecycle policy now requires that pin to be replaced. On a trial run over the identical items with the identical system prompt, the new judge returns a pass rate six points higher. The trend chart is reviewed by the firm's risk committee. How should the migration be handled?

options.text: Adopt the new figure and annotate the chart with the migration date; the newer judge is more capable, so its grades are the more accurate of the two.
Score a stored corpus with both judges, quantify the offset by item type, re-validate the new judge against human labels, and re-baseline the trend.
Adjust the new judge's rubric wording until it reproduces the old judge's pass rate on the same items, so the trend line remains continuous.
Keep the old judge pinned indefinitely, since a stable measurement serves the risk committee better than a current one does.

explanation.correct: Six points of movement with nothing but the judge changed is a calibration shift, and the only defensible response is to measure it. Dual-scoring a stored corpus gives the offset and, more usefully, shows whether it is uniform or concentrated in particular item types — a uniform shift can be described in a footnote, a concentrated one means the new judge grades a specific behaviour differently and the rubric needs attention. Re-validating against the human labels re-establishes that the new judge is right, not merely different, and an explicit break in the series is what stops the committee reading six points of instrument change as improvement.

distractors.A: Capability and calibration are different properties. A more capable judge may be stricter or more lenient than its predecessor, and adopting the number without measuring the offset writes an instrument change into the trend as if it were a quality change.
distractors.C: Tuning the new judge to reproduce the old judge's aggregate makes the old standard the target, errors included. Matching a marginal pass rate also does not imply matching item-level verdicts: the two judges could agree on the total and disagree on which items pass.
distractors.D: The policy has removed this option, and refusing a scheduled migration converts a manageable planned re-baseline into a forced one under time pressure later. Instruments have lifecycles; the answer is to manage the transition, not to avoid it.

explanation.concept: Treat the grader as a versioned instrument. Any change to judge model, judge prompt or rubric breaks comparability with everything scored before it. Overlap the two graders on a stored corpus, publish the offset, revalidate against human labels, and mark the discontinuity on the chart rather than letting it read as a result.
explanation.tip: When a metric moves and the only thing that changed is how it is measured, the answer always involves running old and new instruments over the same data. Keeping graded outputs on disk is what makes that possible later.

topic: What a bootstrap interval provides on an eval metric
stem: What does a bootstrap confidence interval on an eval metric give you that a normal-approximation interval may not?

options.text: A systematically narrower interval, because resampling extracts more information out of the same set of graded items.
Protection against a biased grader, because resampling averages the grader's individual errors out across many replicates.
A correct interval even when the eval items are correlated, because resampling automatically preserves the correlation structure in the graded data.
An interval for statistics whose sampling distribution is not near normal — medians, ratios, composites — with no closed-form standard error.

explanation.correct: The normal approximation needs a formula for the standard error and needs the statistic to be roughly normally distributed. Plenty of things eval reports actually use are neither: the median latency-adjusted score, a ratio of two rates, a weighted composite of several rubric components, a metric computed after a filtering step. Resampling the observed data and recomputing the statistic on each replicate gives the sampling distribution empirically, which is why it is the general-purpose tool when the metric is not a simple proportion or mean.

distractors.A: Bootstrap intervals are not systematically narrower. They estimate the same uncertainty by a different route and tend to be slightly wider on small samples, which is usually the more honest result.
distractors.B: Every replicate is drawn from the same graded outcomes, so any systematic grader error is present in all of them. Resampling quantifies sampling variability and is completely blind to bias in the measurement itself.
distractors.C: Only if you resample the correlated unit. Drawing individual items from a clustered set reproduces the same over-narrow interval; the clustering has to be built into the resampling scheme deliberately, by resampling documents, sessions or customers instead.

explanation.concept: Reach for the bootstrap when the statistic is awkward, not when the answer is inconvenient. It handles non-normal and formula-free statistics and it can handle clustering, but only if the resampling unit matches the unit of dependence in the data. It never corrects bias in the underlying measurement.
explanation.tip: Distinguish variance from bias on every statistics option. Resampling, larger samples and repeated grading all address variance; only an independent reference addresses bias.

topic: Run metadata needed to reproduce a reported eval score
stem: An internal audit of a government department's AI register finds that a pass rate quoted in a ministerial briefing six months ago cannot be reproduced. The eval pipeline stored the resulting score and nothing else. Which records would have made that run reproducible? (Choose THREE.)

options.text: The eval set version identifier and the exact list of item ids scored in the run.
The names of the engineers who reviewed the run output before it was quoted.
The prompt version, model identifier and generation settings used to produce the outputs.
The judge prompt version, judge model identifier and grading settings used to score them.
The wall-clock duration of the run and the total token spend it incurred.

explanation.correct: A score is the output of three things: what was asked, what answered, and what graded. The item set fixes the first, the prompt version with its model and generation settings fixes the second, and the judge prompt with its model and grading settings fixes the third. Miss any one and the number cannot be regenerated, and — more damagingly for an audit — a later disagreement cannot be attributed. Recording all three is what turns a reported figure into a claim someone can check rather than a number someone remembers producing.

distractors.B: Reviewer identity is an accountability record and belongs in the register for that reason. It contributes nothing to regenerating the number: knowing who signed it off does not tell you what was scored or how.
distractors.E: Duration and spend are operational telemetry, useful for capacity and budget conversations. Neither is an input to the score, so neither helps reproduce it.

explanation.concept: Treat an eval run as an experiment whose full configuration is part of the result. Version and record the item set, the system configuration and the grader configuration together with the score, and store the raw graded outputs. Without the grader configuration in particular, you cannot later distinguish a real change from an instrument change.
explanation.tip: Sort candidate metadata into inputs to the number versus facts about the run. Only the inputs reproduce it, and there are exactly three families of them: items, system, grader.

topic: Grading needs a model judge should not be used for
stem: A defence-electronics manufacturer is designing the eval for a Claude step that turns engineering specifications into technician test-procedure checklists. The eval budget allows a rubric judge on every item. For which of these grading needs is a model judge the wrong instrument? (Choose TWO.)

options.text: Deciding whether the ordering of steps in the checklist is logically coherent given the dependencies in the specification.
Confirming that every part number cited in the checklist exists in the manufacturer's parts master file.
Judging whether the wording of each step is clear enough for a technician with roughly two years' experience.
Assessing whether a safety caveat that the specification implies but does not state explicitly has been included.
Verifying that the checklist's stated total duration equals the sum of the durations it gives for the individual steps.

explanation.correct: Both keys are decidable by code against an authoritative source: a set membership test against the parts master, and an addition. Routing them to a model means paying more for a stochastic answer to a question with a determinate one, accepting that the grader can be wrong, and forfeiting the ability to name exactly which part number or which arithmetic failed. The other three all require weighing evidence against a standard that cannot be written as a predicate, which is precisely the work a rubric judge exists to do.

distractors.A: Dependency coherence is a judgement over the semantics of a specification. There is no lookup table for whether calibrating before mounting is wrong in this context, so a rubric judge reading the spec alongside the checklist is the appropriate instrument.
distractors.C: Audience-appropriate clarity is inherently a rubric judgement, and one that should be anchored with worked examples of what clear enough looks like for that experience level. No deterministic check decides it.
distractors.D: Detecting an implied but unstated requirement is the hardest form of judgement in this list, and the least amenable to a rule. It also deserves a validated judge and human spot-checks given the safety consequence, but a model judge is still the right kind of instrument.

explanation.concept: Use the cheapest instrument that decides the question. Anything checkable against a system of record, a schema, or arithmetic belongs in code: exact, free, reproducible, and immune to judge drift. Reserve the model judge for properties that require weighing evidence, and let the deterministic layer run first so the judge only sees what survives.
explanation.tip: Scan each candidate criterion for an authoritative external source or a closed-form computation. If one exists, a model judge is the wrong tool no matter how comfortably it could answer.

topic: Responding to a saturated eval suite
stem: A cosmetics retailer's ingredient-question assistant scores 99% on its 250-item eval suite and has done so for the last five releases. Over the same period the customer-support team has escalated a steady stream of incorrect allergen answers, none of which resemble anything in the suite. The eval currently gates release. What should the team do next?

options.text: Treat the suite as saturated: source new items from the escalations and uncovered traffic, and check they separate two prompt versions before gating.
Tighten the judge's rubric on the existing 250 items until the pass rate falls back into a range where release-to-release movement is clearly visible.
Continue reporting the 99% and route the allergen escalations into a separate manual quality process, since the two measure different things.
Reduce the suite to the handful of items that still fail occasionally, so the reported pass rate has room to move between releases.

explanation.correct: A gate that has returned the same near-perfect number for five releases while real failures accumulate is no longer gating anything; it has stopped covering the part of the task where the system is weak. The escalations are free, high-quality, production-sourced evidence of exactly that gap, so they are the right source for new items. The step teams skip is the last one: after adding items, check that the enlarged suite actually distinguishes two prompt versions you already believe differ. A suite that cannot separate anything is not a gate whatever its score.

distractors.B: Turning up strictness lowers the number without adding a single case the suite did not already contain. The system's real weakness is in allergen questions the set does not include, and no amount of severity on the existing 250 items will surface those.
distractors.C: This formalises the eval's irrelevance. Accepting a permanent parallel manual process means release decisions are made on a number known not to reflect quality, and the manual process becomes the real gate without ever being designed as one.
distractors.D: A failures-only subset cannot detect a regression in the behaviour that currently works, which is most of what a change can break, and its pass rate is not comparable with anything previously reported to the business.

explanation.concept: An eval suite has a shelf life. Once a system saturates it, the suite measures nothing further and must be extended from sources that reflect current failures — escalations, complaints, uncovered traffic. Validate any extension by checking it discriminates between versions you already know differ; discriminating power, not item count, is what a gate needs.
explanation.tip: A flat, near-ceiling score alongside a live stream of real-world failures is always a coverage problem. Beware options that make the number look better without changing what the suite contains.

topic: Limitation of n-gram overlap metrics for abstractive summaries
stem: For evaluating abstractive summaries against a single human reference summary, what is the central limitation of n-gram overlap metrics such as ROUGE?

options.text: They are too expensive to run over a large eval set, because the overlap computation is quadratic in the summary length.
They cannot be computed at all when the candidate summary is longer than either the reference summary or the source document.
They measure surface word overlap, so a faithful paraphrase scores low while an unfaithful copy of the reference's wording scores high.
They are undefined for candidates shorter than the reference summary, which systematically biases the metric against concise output.

explanation.correct: Overlap metrics answer how much of the reference's vocabulary reappears, which is only loosely related to whether the summary is true and complete. Both error directions follow: paraphrase is punished even when the content is perfect, and a summary that lifts the reference's phrasing while inverting a fact or dropping a qualifier can score well. That is fatal for the property most summarisation evals actually care about, which is faithfulness to the source. Overlap remains useful as a cheap regression tripwire, where a sudden collapse is informative even though the absolute value is not.

distractors.A: Overlap scoring is a cheap string operation, and low cost is one of the few genuine advantages these metrics have. Expense is the argument against model grading, not against overlap.
distractors.B: Nothing about the relative lengths of candidate, reference and source prevents computation. The metric is defined for any pair of strings, however implausible.
distractors.D: The metric is defined at any length. Recall-oriented variants do penalise brevity, which is a real weighting effect worth knowing, but it is a consequence of which variant you chose rather than the central limitation.

explanation.concept: Choose a metric that measures the property you care about. For summarisation that property is usually faithfulness and coverage, which surface overlap does not track. Use overlap as an inexpensive tripwire alongside a rubric judge that checks claims against the source, and validate the judge against human labels.
explanation.tip: For any automatic metric, construct the two adversarial cases in your head: an output that is right but scores low, and one that is wrong but scores high. If both are easy to construct, the metric cannot carry a ship decision.

topic: Sizing the human-labelled sample that validates a judge
stem: A credit union wants to replace its manual quality sampling of member-message drafts with an LLM judge. Its risk function will accept the change only if the team can state judge–human agreement to within about ±5 percentage points at 95% confidence. Roughly 8% of drafts currently fail manual QA. Human labelling is the binding cost. What does this require?

options.text: Around 400 human-labelled items, which is what a ±5-point interval on a proportion needs, drawn so that enough of them are failures.
Around 100 human-labelled items, since agreement is expected to be high and proportions near 1 have lower variance than proportions near 0.5.
Around 1,500 human-labelled items, matching the size of the main eval run so that the two figures are directly comparable to one another.
Sample size is not the binding constraint: label any convenient number with two humans as well, since human–human agreement bounds judge–human agreement.

explanation.correct: A 95% interval of ±5 points on a proportion needs about (1.96/0.05)² × 0.25 ≈ 385 observations, so roughly 400 is the number the stated precision buys. The second half matters just as much. At an 8% failure rate a random 400 contains about 32 failures, and the agreement statistic will be dominated by easy passes, so the block has to be composed deliberately to put enough failures in front of both the humans and the judge. Precision and composition are separate requirements and the risk function's condition is only met when both are satisfied.

distractors.B: One hundred items gives roughly ±10 points on a proportion near the middle, and still around ±6 even at 0.9 — too wide to separate an acceptable grader from an unacceptable one. Assuming high agreement in order to justify a smaller sample assumes the thing being tested.
distractors.C: Matching the main run's size is a rule of thumb with no basis. Validation sample size follows from the precision required on the agreement estimate; the main run's size follows from the effect it must detect. The two answer different questions and there is no reason for them to coincide.
distractors.D: Human–human agreement is worth measuring and is a genuine ceiling on what any grader can achieve on the construct. It does not substitute for estimating judge–human agreement, and it says nothing about how precisely that estimate is known, which is exactly what the risk function asked for.

explanation.concept: Grader validation is a measurement with its own precision requirement, so size it from the interval width you must report, not from the size of anything else. Then check composition: on a skewed task, a sample that satisfies the precision arithmetic can still be uninformative about the minority class that matters.
explanation.tip: Memorise the anchor: about 400 observations gives roughly ±5 points, about 100 gives roughly ±10, and precision improves only with the square root of sample size.

topic: Reporting a defensible score from a stochastic system
stem: A water utility's leak-report triage assistant is evaluated with a suite that reports one pass rate per run. Re-running the identical suite against the identical prompt on three consecutive occasions returned 84%, 87% and 82%. The board's quarterly pack shows only the most recent figure, and last quarter's pack showed 82%. Which changes make the reported number defensible? (Choose TWO.)

options.text: Run the suite several times per configuration and report the mean with its spread, so readers can separate a real move from run-to-run noise.
Report the highest of the three runs, on the grounds that it represents what the system has demonstrably shown it can do.
Restrict the suite to the items whose outcome is stable across repeated runs, so the reported quarterly figure stops moving.
Reduce generation variability where the configuration allows it, and state the sampling settings used alongside the score.
Grow the eval set until the run-to-run spread disappears entirely, which removes the need to report variability at all.

explanation.correct: A five-point spread across identical runs means the board has been shown a number whose noise is larger than most of the differences it is being asked to interpret. Two complementary fixes apply. Reporting a mean with its spread makes the uncertainty visible, so a three-point quarterly move is read as noise rather than as a decline. Reducing generation variability where the configuration allows shrinks the noise at source and, stated alongside the score, tells the reader which configuration the number belongs to.

distractors.B: Selecting the maximum of several runs is a best-of-k report on the aggregate. It is biased upward by construction, and the bias grows with the number of runs, so a team that runs the suite more often will appear to be improving.
distractors.C: Items with unstable outcomes are the marginal cases, which are the most informative items in the suite. Removing them stabilises the number by discarding the evidence about where the system is borderline.
distractors.E: A larger set does narrow the spread of the aggregate, but it does not go to zero, and part of this spread reflects genuine behavioural variability that the board should know about. Growing the set until variability can be ignored is neither achievable nor the right goal.

explanation.concept: A score from a stochastic system is an estimate with two sources of variation: which items were sampled and what the system did on them this time. Report both by running repeats and publishing the spread, and reduce the second where configuration permits. Any single number quoted without a spread invites readers to interpret noise as signal.
explanation.tip: If a stem shows you the same configuration producing different scores, every option that produces a single stable-looking number by discarding information is wrong. The answer surfaces the variability rather than hiding it.

topic: Seeded defective outputs as a continuous grader check
stem: Some eval pipelines include a small number of deliberately defective outputs whose correct grade is known in advance, scored on every run alongside the real ones. What does that add?

options.text: It raises the overall difficulty of the suite so that the headline pass rate lands in a more discriminating range between releases.
It is a standing check on the grader: if the judge passes an output built to violate a named criterion, the grading pipeline is broken.
It supplies negative examples the prompt can be tuned against, improving the system's handling of similar cases in production traffic.
It establishes the empirical floor of the achievable score range, so the reported pass rate can be normalised against that floor.

explanation.correct: The seeded items are instrumentation for the instrument. Their expected grade is known, so every run silently re-tests the grading path: rubric edits that changed meaning, a judge prompt truncated by a template change, a criterion that stopped firing after a refactor, a judge model swap that shifted the standard. Each of those produces a plausible-looking headline number with nothing to indicate anything is wrong. A seeded defect that suddenly passes is an unambiguous alarm, and it costs a handful of items per run.

distractors.A: A handful of seeded items barely moves the pass rate, and moving the pass rate is not the aim. They are excluded from the system's reported result precisely so that they do not distort it.
distractors.C: Tuning the prompt against items whose purpose is to test the grader contaminates both roles at once: the system learns the seeded defects and the seeded defects stop detecting grader failures. Instrumentation must stay out of the improvement loop.
distractors.D: Pass rates already sit on a fixed zero-to-one scale and need no empirical floor. Normalising the reported result against grader diagnostics would mix two unrelated measurements into one number.

explanation.concept: Instrument the grading pipeline, not just the system. Known-answer canaries with a known expected verdict, run every time, catch silent grader breakage that a headline score cannot reveal. Keep them out of the reported result and out of any set used to tune the system.
explanation.tip: Ask what would happen if the grader broke quietly. Suites with no known-answer items would report a normal-looking number indefinitely, which is why this control exists.

topic: Evaluating a self-reported confidence that drives routing
stem: A veterinary telemedicine platform's Claude step returns a triage recommendation together with a stated confidence of high, medium or low. The routing logic sends every low-confidence case to a duty vet and auto-sends the rest. The current eval reports only overall recommendation accuracy, and it is 91%. Which statements about what this eval is failing to measure are correct? (Choose TWO.)

options.text: Confidence can be evaluated by checking that the model reports high confidence on the large majority of cases, since a good system should mostly be confident.
Because the confidence is self-reported by the model, it cannot be evaluated, and the routing logic should be driven by a separately trained classifier instead.
The routing depends entirely on whether accuracy at high confidence genuinely exceeds accuracy at low confidence, so the eval must report accuracy per level.
Overall accuracy already accounts for the confidence signal, because miscalibrated confidence would show up as a lower overall accuracy figure on the eval.
A system can be well calibrated and inaccurate, or accurate and badly calibrated; since routing consumes the confidence, calibration needs its own metric and threshold.

explanation.correct: The confidence label is not decoration here — it decides whether a vet ever sees the case. Its usefulness rests entirely on separation: accuracy in the high bucket has to be materially better than in the low bucket, or the routing is sending the wrong cases to the vet while auto-sending errors. That is measured by conditioning accuracy on the stated level. And because calibration is logically independent of accuracy, it needs its own number and its own bar: 91% overall is compatible with a system whose confidence carries no information at all.

distractors.A: Reporting high confidence often is a property of the model's disposition, not evidence that the confidence is informative. A system that says high on everything has a perfectly high confidence rate and a completely useless routing signal.
distractors.B: Self-reported confidence is straightforwardly evaluable: bucket the outputs by stated level and compare accuracy within each bucket against outcomes. Whether to replace it with a separate classifier is a design decision that should follow the measurement, not substitute for it.
distractors.D: Overall accuracy is computed across all cases and is completely insensitive to how the errors are distributed across confidence levels. Two systems with identical 91% accuracy can have opposite routing behaviour, one concentrating its errors in the low bucket and one in the high.

explanation.concept: Every signal a downstream component consumes needs its own eval. When a confidence, a category or a flag drives routing, escalation or suppression, measure the property that makes it useful — usually conditional accuracy across its levels — and set an acceptance threshold on it. Overall accuracy on the primary output says nothing about it.
explanation.tip: Trace what each field of the output is used for. Any field that changes downstream behaviour is an eval target in its own right, and its absence from the eval is usually the intended answer.

topic: What should determine an eval acceptance threshold
stem: An eval's acceptance threshold — the score at which a version is permitted to ship — should be derived principally from what?

options.text: The score the current production version achieves on the same suite, so that no release ever ships worse than the incumbent does.
A conventional level such as 90%, adjusted upward or downward according to how difficult the task is judged to be.
The highest score any candidate version has achieved so far, so that the bar ratchets upward as the system improves.
The consequence of the residual errors at that score: what the failures cost, who absorbs them, and which control catches them.

explanation.correct: A threshold is a statement about tolerable residual risk, so it has to be derived from what the errors below it do. Ninety percent means one failure in ten reaching whatever sits downstream, and whether that is acceptable depends entirely on whether the downstream is a human reviewer, a retry, or a customer. Deriving the number this way also produces the argument that goes with it, which is what lets an architect defend the bar to a risk committee and revisit it when a downstream control is added or removed.

distractors.A: A non-regression rule is a sound secondary gate and most suites should have one. As the primary basis it enshrines the incumbent's error rate as acceptable indefinitely, and it gives no answer at all at first launch, when there is no incumbent to compare against.
distractors.B: A round number imported from elsewhere carries no information about this task. Ninety percent can be far too lax where each failure costs a customer relationship, and unreachable where two experts only agree eight times in ten about what correct means.
distractors.C: Ratcheting to the best observed score makes the bar a moving target set by whichever run got lucky. It also blocks changes that trade a point of accuracy for a large gain in latency, cost or maintainability, which are frequently the right trades.

explanation.concept: Set thresholds from consequence, not from convention or from history. State the bar together with what happens to the failures beneath it and which control absorbs them; that pairing is what makes the number reviewable. Non-regression against the incumbent belongs alongside it as a second, separate gate.
explanation.tip: Any option that sets a threshold from another number — the incumbent's, the best-ever, an industry convention — is deriving the bar from the wrong place. Look for the one that reasons from what the residual failures do.

topic: Systematic disagreement between a deterministic check and a judge
stem: A parcel carrier's address-normalisation eval runs two graders over every item: a deterministic check that validates the returned postcode against the national address file, and a rubric judge that assesses whether the normalised address is usable for delivery. On 8% of items the deterministic check fails while the judge passes. The suite currently reports the judge's pass rate as the headline. What should the eval lead do next?

options.text: Treat the deterministic check as authoritative for the postcode, then hand-review a sample of the judge's passes on those items to find the cause.
Take the disjunction and pass an item if either grader passes it, since requiring both to agree imposes a stricter bar than the delivery task needs.
Remove the deterministic check, since the rubric judge already assesses deliverability and two overlapping graders create the double-counting problem.
Take the conjunction of the two graders, report the lower combined number, and treat the disputed 8% as failures without investigating.

explanation.correct: A systematic 8% disagreement between two graders is the most informative thing in the run, and it has two possible readings that lead to different actions. Either the judge is failing to notice invalid postcodes, in which case the judge needs a rubric change and every historical judge score is suspect; or the rubric is passing those items on a genuinely different criterion, in which case the two graders are measuring different properties and both belong in the report separately. Hand-reviewing a sample of the 8% distinguishes them cheaply, and until it is done the headline pass rate cannot be interpreted.

distractors.B: The disjunction lets the weaker grader override the stronger one on a property the stronger one decides exactly against an authoritative file. It guarantees a higher pass rate and a less meaningful one, and it makes the deterministic check pointless.
distractors.C: A rubric judge does not subsume a validator; it is a stochastic reader of a property that a lookup settles. Overlapping criteria inside one rubric is a distinct problem from layering a deterministic check beneath a judge, which is a sound design.
distractors.D: Conjunction is very likely the right end state and the combined number is the honest one. Adopting it without looking at the 8% discards direct evidence about grader quality and leaves a possible defect in the judge unexamined and still running.

explanation.concept: Where two graders assess overlapping properties, their disagreement rate is a free diagnostic on both. Investigate systematic disagreement before choosing an aggregation rule: the pattern tells you whether one grader is wrong or whether they are measuring different things, and those call for opposite responses.
explanation.tip: When a stem gives two graders and a disagreement percentage, the intended action is to characterise the disagreement, never to pick an aggregation rule that makes it disappear.

topic: Macro versus micro averaging over unequal eval categories
stem: An eval covers ten task categories of very unequal size. What distinguishes a macro-average from a micro-average of the per-category results, and when does the choice matter?

options.text: Macro-averaging weights each item equally and micro-averaging weights each category equally; the two diverge only when the categories differ in pass rate.
Macro-averaging weights each category equally and micro-averaging weights each item equally, so they diverge when small and large categories differ.
The two are equivalent for a simple pass rate and differ only for precision and recall, where the denominators are class-conditional.
Micro-averaging should be used for eval reporting in all cases, because it is the unbiased estimate of performance on live production traffic.

explanation.correct: Micro-averaging pools all items and computes one rate, so every item counts once and the largest categories dominate. Macro-averaging computes a rate per category and averages those, so every category counts once regardless of size. On a set with ten unequal categories they can differ substantially, and the difference is itself informative: a macro figure well below the micro figure means the small categories are the weak ones. Reporting both, with the per-category breakdown behind them, is how you avoid the choice becoming a way of hiding a result.

distractors.A: The definitions are reversed. Micro pools items and therefore weights items equally; macro averages category scores and therefore weights categories equally. The condition for divergence is also incomplete — unequal category sizes are required as well as unequal rates.
distractors.C: They diverge for any metric computed over groups of unequal size, pass rate very much included. The distinction concerns how the groups are weighted, not which metric is being averaged over them.
distractors.D: Micro-averaging does estimate the traffic-weighted figure, which is often what production cares about, but that is exactly why it conceals small categories. Declaring it always correct discards the reason macro-averaging exists.

explanation.concept: State the weighting whenever you report an aggregate over groups. Micro answers what a random request experiences; macro answers how the system performs across the kinds of work it does. Neither is the truth on its own, and where any category must not fail, macro belongs on the front page next to micro.
explanation.tip: Reversed-definition options are common in this exam. Fix which one pools raw items in your memory — micro pools items — and the rest of the option falls out from it.
